batches.framing_correction: The question asked about optogenetics used to inject false memories in MICE. No 2025-2026 mouse false-memory optogenetics paper was found in the indexes searched. The two recent papers fitting the description are both Drosophila (N83, N84), and N83 is its own antidote: the false memory came from manipulating reminder cues, not from writing with light, and the authors' null control found that circuit activation during reminders in untrained flies induced nothing. The artefacts therefore cover the fly work AND the foundational mouse work, and name the species in every sentence that makes a claim.
batches.verification_method: Every DOI resolved against the Crossref REST API (api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}) on 2026-10-18, with returned title, first-author family name, year, venue and volume/pages compared against the claim written here. Where a DOI was not already known, it was obtained by Crossref query.bibliographic title search or from a PubMed/Europe PMC record — never guessed. Abstract text and species/preparation details were read from PubMed efetch or Europe PMC resultType=core; full text was read for the one paper whose framing is most load-bearing (Yang et al. 2026, open access at PMC13533848).
batches.schema_decision: evidence.tier was NOT changed on any entry. The seven tiers in src/lib/evidence-tiers.ts grade evidence strength and carry no species: demonstrated_lab renders as 'Demonstrated' and names no organism. Moving a tier to encode species would change what every other entry's tier means, so two descriptive fields, tara.clinical.species_of_evidence and tara.clinical.preparation, were added under the registrar's existing schema_extensions mechanism and the tiers were left as derived. Whether the tier vocabulary should gain a species dimension is an open ruling, recorded as optogen2-find-001.

Liu X, Ramirez S, Pang PT, Puryear CB, Govindarajan A, Deisseroth K, Tonegawa S. Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall. Nature 484:381-385, 2012. Species: Mouse. Preparation: Transgenic c-fos-tTA mice with viral AAV9-TRE-ChR2-EYFP injected into dentate gyrus; doxycycline-off activity-dependent tagging during fear conditioning; implanted optical fibre for blue-light delivery to DG. Invasive: stereotaxic viral injection plus chronic fibre implant. Claim in the authors' own words: 'Here we show in mice that optogenetic reactivation of hippocampal neurons activated during fear conditioning is sufficient to induce freezing behaviour.' And: 'activating a sparse but specific ensemble of hippocampal neurons that contribute to a memory engram is sufficient for the recall of that memory.' What it does not claim: It does not claim a memory was created or its content inspected. It is a SUFFICIENCY claim about recall of an already-formed memory. The behavioural readout is freezing. Why it matters here: Establishes that a sparse tagged ensemble is a sufficient causal handle on a behavioural memory output — the existence proof that ensemble-level write access can drive behaviour, under laboratory access conditions no deployed BCI has.

items.summary: Ramirez S, Liu X, Lin P-A, Suh J, Pignatelli M, Redondo RL, Ryan TJ, Tonegawa S. Creating a False Memory in the Hippocampus. Science 341:387-391, 2013. Species: Mouse. Preparation: c-fos-tTA mice, AAV-TRE-ChR2-EYFP in dentate gyrus or CA1, doxycycline-gated tagging of cells active in context A, implanted fibre; optical reactivation during foot-shock in context B. Claim in the authors' own words: 'We created a false memory in mice by optogenetically manipulating memory engram-bearing cells in the hippocampus... The DG experimental group showed increased freezing in the original context, in which a foot shock was never delivered... Our data demonstrate that it is possible to generate an internally represented and behaviorally expressed fear memory via artificial means.' What it does not claim: The authors' own operational definition of the 'false memory' is a context-specific freezing response to a context where no shock occurred. It is an artificially formed ASSOCIATION between a pre-existing contextual representation and an aversive event. Nothing in the paper claims a detailed episodic narrative, scene content, or any specified experience was inserted. The popular 'implanted a false memory' phrasing comes from the title and press coverage, not from a content-level claim. Why it matters here: The canonical citation for 'an association can be formed that does not correspond to events', and therefore the paper most likely to be misread downstream; its own operational definition is the correction.

items.summary: Redondo RL, Kim J, Arons AL, Ramirez S, Liu X, Tonegawa S. Bidirectional switch of the valence associated with a hippocampal contextual memory engram. Nature 513:426-430, 2014. Species: Mouse. Preparation: c-fos-tTA mice, ChR2 labelling of cells active during contextual fear or reward conditioning in dorsal DG or basolateral amygdala; implanted fibre; optogenetic place-avoidance and place-preference tests. Claim in the authors' own words: 'although the DG-engram group displayed a response indicating a switch of the memory valence, the BLA-engram group did not... the neurons carrying the memory engram of a given neutral context have plasticity such that the valence of a conditioned response evoked by their reactivation can be reversed by re-associating this contextual memory engram with a new unconditioned stimulus of an opposite valence.' What it does not claim: Valence re-assignment is not content rewriting, and it is not general: it worked at the DG (contextual representation) and failed at the BLA (valence-carrying structure). The anatomical asymmetry is the result. Why it matters here: Shows that the manipulable variable at the hippocampal site is the valence attached to a representation, and that the same manipulation fails at a neighbouring structure — i.e. site specificity, not a general 'rewrite' capability.

Claim in the authors' own words: 'Using optogenetic stimulation without any sensory input in mice, we found that an artificial association between stored, non-related contextual, and fear information was generated through the synchronous activation of distinct cell ensembles corresponding to the stored information. This artificial association shared characteristics with physiologically associated memories, such as N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor activity and protein synthesis dependence.' What it does not claim: The information associated was ALREADY STORED. The manipulation links two pre-existing ensembles; it does not write new content. The authors' own framing is 'association of information... achieved through the synchronous activity of distinct cell ensembles'. Why it matters here: The clearest statement of the actual primitive: synchrony between two already-encoded ensembles. Any threat model should describe the capability as ensemble co-activation, not content injection.

items.summary: Yang W, Zattera B, Pavão-Delgado M, Warnecke C, Schweizer JA, Ricciuti A, Çoban B, Felsenberg J. Creating true and false memories from forgotten information in Drosophila. Nature Neuroscience 29:2204-2213, 2026. Species: Drosophila melanogaster (vinegar fly). NOT mouse. NOT mammal. Preparation: Genetically modified flies (GAL4/UAS). Three intervention tools: thermogenetic activation via dTRPA1 (whole-animal heating to 32 °C during odour presentation), optogenetic activation via CsChrimson (red light, 634 nm, 500 Hz, 25 µW/mm², whole-animal illumination), and Shibire-ts1 temperature-sensitive synaptic blockade. Light delivery is whole-animal external illumination of a transparent-cuticle insect — there is no implanted fibre and no cranial window, because the preparation does not need one. Claim in the authors' own words: 'Here we show in Drosophila that reminder cues recover forgotten aversive memories. Forgotten memories persist as silent memory traces in behaviorally neutral mushroom body output neurons. From this silent state, reminders recover memory expression by reinstating the original memory trace in mushroom body output neurons that guide behavior. However, manipulating reminders can distort recovery, leading to false memory formation. The effectiveness of this distortion depends on whether misleading reminder cues were present during the original training event. Both true memory recovery and false memory formation are context-dependent processes gated by separable dopaminergic pathways.' Why it matters here: The most likely source of a 2026 'false memories implanted' headline, and the strongest available correction to it: the species is a fly, the false memory comes from misleading cues, and direct circuit activation alone produced no memory at all.

items.summary: Tumkaya T, Zhang X, Mai Y, Stewart J, Claridge-Chang A. Entirely synthetic memory inception via dual optogenetic activation of sensory and dopaminergic neurons. iScience 28:113540, 2025. Species: Drosophila melanogaster (vinegar fly). NOT mouse. Preparation: Transgenic flies expressing optogenetic actuators in olfactory sensory neurons and in dopaminergic reinforcement neurons; external light delivery; no implant. Claim in the authors' own words: 'We addressed this by optogenetically replacing natural stimuli—odor-evoked activity, punishment, and reward signals—either individually or in combination. Notably, even in a full-substitution paradigm where both olfactory and reinforcement signals were replaced, optogenetic activation successfully implanted synthetic memories. Our findings demonstrate that simple coincident activation of sensory and neuromodulatory neurons is enough to instruct associative memory formation—complex temporal or ensemble activity patterns characteristic of natural stimuli are not required.' What it does not claim: The 'synthetic memory' is an odour-valence association assembled by co-activating a sensory channel and a reinforcement channel. It is association formation from scratch in an invertebrate, not episodic content. 'Implanted' here means the CS and US were both replaced by light. Why it matters here: The strongest 'built an association entirely out of stimulation' result found in this pass, and the clearest demonstration that the requirement is coincidence rather than naturalistic pattern fidelity — relevant to how little precision a write primitive would need, in a preparation with no mammalian analogue.

items.summary: Hu S, Yang J, Yin S, Zhong Y, An Y, Guo Y, Zhai Z, Zhong Y. Identification of an engram ensemble mediating memory forgetting in the dentate gyrus. Neuron 114:759-773.e5, 2026. Species: Mouse. Preparation: Dual activity-dependent tagging (Fos and Npas4 promoters) in dentate gyrus with optogenetic reactivation; viral transduction plus implanted light delivery. Claim in the authors' own words: 'Reactivation of the Fos-tagged ensemble promotes memory retrieval, whereas reactivation of the Npas4-dependent ensemble drives forgetting, with manipulation of the forgetting ensemble inversely shifting memory ensemble reactivation. Such encoding enables flexibility in recall outcomes, ranging from full-scale memory expression to complete forgetting. Meanwhile, learned information remains unperturbed, as reactivation modifications specifically target the forgetting ensemble.' What it does not claim: Explicitly NOT erasure of content: 'learned information remains unperturbed'. The manipulation changes accessibility, not the stored information. Why it matters here: Identifies a separate ensemble whose activation suppresses recall while leaving the stored information intact — availability rather than integrity, in threat-model terms. This is a genuinely new 2026 handle not present in the 2012-2015 line.

items.summary: Berdugo-Vega G, Sierra C, Astori S, Calati V, Orsat J, Scoglio MJ, Sandi C, Gräff J. Cognitive rejuvenation through partial reprogramming of engram cells. Conversely, targeted volumetric inactivation of these interneurons suppresses context-induced memory retrieval.' What it does not claim: Retrieval gating of an existing remote memory. items.summary: Chen Q, Wu A, Yu B, Chae S, Tan Z, Ramot A, Aljadeff J, Komiyama T. Targeted stimulation of motor cortex ensembles drives learned movements. Nature, 2026. Species: Mouse. Preparation: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging plus holographic optogenetic stimulation of functionally defined M1 layer 2/3 ensembles in head-fixed mice performing a learned lever-press task. Claim in the authors' own words: 'Brief synchronous stimulation of about 20 neurons whose activity onset precedes voluntary movement onset induced movements resembling the learned movement, while producing activity patterns in other M1 neurons resembling the learned activity.' Why it matters here: The best available calibration on how much a precise write buys you: roughly 20 cells can trigger a learned motor pattern, but only when the circuit is already in the right state and only for the right cells. State-dependence is the honest limiting factor, not raw targeting precision.

items.summary: Moore H, Dehnad M, Freelin A, Granger B, Subramanian S, van der Molen T, Kulkarni A, Berto S, Lega BC, Konopka G. Stimulation modulates gene-linked cell assemblies in the human brain. Nature 657:724-734, 2026. Species: HUMAN. Preparation: Ex vivo resected human temporal cortex from patients undergoing neurosurgery, on a platform combining microelectrode-array ELECTRICAL stimulation with simultaneous recording and single-nucleus genomics; plus a comparison with in vivo electrical stimulation in human cortex. NO OPSIN. NO LIGHT. NO GENETIC MODIFICATION OF THE PATIENT. Tissue access came from clinically indicated resection. Claim in the authors' own words: 'we developed an ex vivo platform that integrates microelectrode array stimulation with simultaneous recording and single-nucleus genomics from resected temporal cortex obtained from patients undergoing neurosurgery. We found that stimulation strengthens cell assemblies and then linked this effect to cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks. We further demonstrated the generalizability of these findings by identifying common cell-type-specific gene expression signatures in the human cortex following in vivo stimulation.' What it does not claim: No memory was created, recalled, falsified or re-valenced. No engram was tagged. No optogenetics was used. The readout is assembly strength and transcriptional signature, not memory content. The authors frame the work as a foundation for therapeutic neuromodulation targets. Why it matters here: This is the honest human anchor. It shows electrical stimulation can measurably change human cortical assembly structure and gene regulation — and it simultaneously shows how far that is from engram-level memory manipulation, because it required resected tissue and achieved nothing resembling memory content control.

items.summary: Bunnell B, López FJ, Yuan D, Robinson MR, Duncan JL, Birch DG. Phase I/IIa Study of an Intravitreal Optogenetic Therapy (AGN-151597) in Patients with Advanced Retinitis Pigmentosa. Why it matters here: The real state of human optogenetics in 2026: one organ, one indication, viral delivery to a naturally light-exposed tissue, and no demonstrated functional benefit in this trial. It bounds any inference from animal engram work to people.

However, several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of magnetogenetics and uncovered the underlying mechanisms. 'Noninvasive' here refers to the stimulation modality only — the genetic targeting requirement is unchanged. No memory application is claimed. Why it matters here: The clearest example of why 'non-invasive optogenetics-like control' must be read carefully: it removes the fibre, not the gene delivery, and the authors themselves say it is not yet routine.

items.summary: Brunswick CA, Carpenter CM, Dennis NA, Kwapis JL. Not the same as it ever was: A review of memory modification, updating, and distortion in humans and rodents. items.summary: Shao X, Chen C, Loftus EF, Zhu B. Shared memories of event details in the human brain are altered by misinformation and test expectations. PLOS Biology 24:e3003886, 2026. Species: HUMAN (n=100). Preparation: fMRI across four stages — viewing events, initial free recall, reading misinformation, final free recall. Entirely non-invasive, observational neuroimaging. No stimulation, no transduction, no intervention on the brain. Claim in the authors' own words: 'Misinformation increased the likelihood of people forming shared false memories of event details. People who formed shared false memories exhibited similar detail-specific patterns of activity in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex when reading misinformation.' What it does not claim: The false memory is induced by MISINFORMATION — a stimulus delivered through normal perception. The neural data are correlational pattern similarity. Nothing was done to the brain. Under the project's epistemic rules this is an association, not a causal neural claim, and reverse inference does not apply. Why it matters here: The actually-demonstrated route to a false memory in a human being is misinformation, not neural intervention — which is the single most important calibration in this whole manifest for anyone tempted to treat engram optogenetics as a human attack surface.

held_items.subject: Which publication prompted the question
held_items.why_held: Not determinable. Two 2025-2026 candidates fit a 'false or synthetic memory by optogenetics' description and BOTH are Drosophila (N83, N84). The artefacts therefore cover the fly work and the foundational mouse work, so they are correct either way.

held_items.subject: A 2025-2026 mouse false-memory optogenetics paper
held_items.why_held: SEARCHED, NOT FOUND, reported as a search result and not as a universal negative. A PubMed title/abstract search for ('false memory') AND (optogenetic* OR engram) restricted to 2025-2026 returned zero records; a Europe PMC cross-check over all years returned 157 whose 2025-2026 subset held no such mouse primary paper.

held_items.subject: N81, N82, N92, N93, N101 beyond title level
held_items.why_held: DOI, authors, year and venue verified; abstracts not retrieved. Published at title level only and flagged as such in the catalogue row. N82 additionally carries a published correction (10.1186/s13041-023-01016-y) that must be read before citing.

held_items.subject: Species and preparation for N101 (sonogenetic pacemaker)
held_items.why_held: Only title and author list confirmed. The organ is cardiac, which is outside QIF's neural scope per the 2026-10-17 scope note, so the row is recorded for completeness and used for nothing.

held_items.subject: Any human optogenetic engram or memory manipulation result
held_items.why_held: SEARCHED, NOT FOUND. Every human optogenetics result surfaced was retinal. The nearest human memory-circuit work is electrical stimulation of resected and in vivo cortex measuring assembly strength and gene expression (N96). Treated as no, with no extraordinary evidence found to displace that, and written as a search scope rather than a universal negative.

held_items.subject: Whether the N83 authors state human-translation limits
held_items.why_held: NOT FOUND in the open-access full text. A keyword scan found only a technical limitation of the connectome dataset used. Recorded as an absence, not as a denial: the authors neither claim nor disclaim human relevance.
